newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Poland on guard to avoid C/A crisis - Belka.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Poland on guard to avoid C/A crisis - Belka.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday that foreign direct investment, monetary tightening and the planned leaner 1998 budget should keep Poland clear from the Czech-style financial crisis.

Belka told a news conference that a mix of monetary tightening, crawling zloty devaluation and the planned cut in 1998 budget deficit to below two percent of gross domestic product should ease pressure on the trade and current account balances.

He said Poland, which experiences similar trade pressures as other fast-growing economies, was largely immune to a financial crisis because its external shortfall was offset by long-term direct investment rather than portfolio capital.
"As long as the gap is filled with foreign investments in productive assets there is no danger and this is the case in Poland," Belka said.

"The difference between Poland and the Czech Republic is that our deficit is almost entirely financed by foreign direct investments and only in few percent by short-term capital while in the Czech Republic the proportion was different," he added.

Poland's 1996 foreign direct investment rose $5.19 billion, pushing the amount attracted since 1990 to more than $12 billion. The government's Foreign Investment Agency (PAIZ) says the investment should reach $30 billion by the year 2000.
Belka said so far nothing indicated that Poland's trade gap would exceed $12 billion this year and current account deficit $6 billion, levels predicted before and deemed safe for the economy.
Earlier this week the deputy head of the central bank said that unless the government balanced the budget next year the trade gap could soar to $16 billion -- a level which could threaten stability.
Those concerns were echoed by the International Monetary Fund, whose Warsaw representative also said Poland should further tighten its monetary policy.
But Belka said the central bank and the government have already taken steps to prevent the deficit from getting out of hand next year and considered the tightening sufficient.
"If it turns out that (present policies) are insufficient we will tighten them further, but it may prove unnecessary and I think that (what we have) will be sufficient," he added.
He said it would take time before the market would fully feel the impact of monetary tightening resulting from increased mandatory reserves and rising real interest rates.

"I sometimes get an impression that I have more faith in monetary policy and its mid-term effect than those responsible for it and I think we expect spectacular effects of monetary policy too soon," he said, apparently referring to the central bank's warnings.
Belka declined to say whether the finance ministry would suggest an official interest rate rise to the central bank.
"The central bank is independent and I won't be suggesting anything through the media, we are in talks and if adjustments are needed we will make them," he said.

Belka dismissed the proposal to balance the budget already next year and brushed off some analysts' suggestions that fear of voter backlash at parliamentary polls in September kept the ruling left from tightening budget purse strings.
He said getting rid of the deficit over such a short time was impossible because there was not enough flexibility in the way budget spending and revenues were planned.
